september-11.summary: Four hijacked aircraft killed 2,977 people in New York, at the Pentagon and in a Pennsylvania field, and produced a reordering of American law, borders and foreign policy that outlasted the presidency that began it.
september-11.significance: The two decades of war that followed killed vastly more people than the attack did, in countries that had not carried it out.

iraq-war.summary: An invasion by the United States and its allies removed Saddam Hussein in three weeks and then occupied the country for eight years, through an insurgency and a sectarian civil war whose consequences included the conditions for the Islamic State.
iraq-war.note: The stated justification - Iraqi weapons of mass destruction - proved to be unfounded, which is not disputed. The death toll is: documented civilian deaths pass 200,000, while survey-based estimates of total excess deaths run several times higher and are argued over on method.

image.credit: Technical Sergeant John L. Houghton, Jr., United States Air Force

social-media.summary: Networks where users supply the content and an algorithm chooses who sees it, which within a decade carried a substantial share of the world's news, politics, advertising and social life.
social-media.significance: The first communications medium where the sorting is done by software optimising for attention. What that has done to politics and to teenagers is argued over with real evidence on more than one side.
social-media.note: The bracket opens between Facebook in 2004 and Twitter in 2006; earlier networks existed and did not reach the scale. Claims about its effects on mental health and on democracy are contested in the literature rather than settled, and this entry does not settle them either.

financial-crisis-2008.summary: American mortgage losses propagated through securitised debt into a banking collapse and the deepest global recession since the 1930s — met with bank rescues, a decade of austerity in much of Europe, and a politics that has not gone back to what it was.
financial-crisis-2008.note: The bracket opens in August 2007, when BNP Paribas froze three funds and interbank lending seized, rather than at the Lehman failure in September 2008 that is usually remembered as the start.

m-pesa.summary: A Kenyan service that let anyone with a basic phone send money by text, turning airtime agents into a banking network and giving tens of millions their first account of any kind.
m-pesa.significance: Banking reached people the banks had never reached, on handsets that were not smartphones, in a country with few branches. It was copied across Africa and South Asia long before the rich world had anything comparable.
m-pesa.note: Kept open because it is infrastructure in daily use rather than an episode that closed. By the late 2010s a sum equivalent to around half of Kenyan GDP was moving through it each year.

smartphone.summary: A pocket computer with a camera, a satellite receiver and a permanent network connection, which went from a luxury to the default way most people on Earth use a computer at all.
smartphone.significance: Within fifteen years most of humanity was carrying a networked computer, and the industries of photography, navigation, music, retail, taxis and news were rebuilt around that fact.
smartphone.note: Not the first: Nokia, BlackBerry and IBM's Simon all put computing on a phone before this. The 2007 iPhone is the bracket's opening because the touchscreen-plus-app-store pattern it set is the one every later device copied, not because it invented the category.

aadhaar.summary: A biometric identity number issued to over a billion Indians, the largest such system ever built, used to route subsidies and payments directly to individuals.
aadhaar.note: Genuinely two-sided. It gave hundreds of millions a usable identity and cut leakage from welfare transfers; it has also produced documented exclusion when biometrics fail for manual labourers and the elderly, and the Supreme Court in 2018 upheld it for state benefits while striking down its mandatory use by private companies.

arab-spring.summary: A Tunisian street vendor's self-immolation in December 2010 set off protests that removed the rulers of Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen, and were met elsewhere with concessions, repression or civil war.
arab-spring.significance: Four governments fell in two years. A decade later Tunisia alone had kept anything like the result, and Syria, Libya and Yemen were at war.

south-sudan-independence.summary: The world's newest widely recognised country, created by referendum after two civil wars spanning half a century, and in civil war again within two years.

crispr.summary: A bacterial immune mechanism repurposed into a cheap, precise way of cutting and rewriting DNA in any organism, and now the basis of approved treatments for inherited disease.
crispr.significance: Editing a genome went from a specialist project to something a graduate student could do in a week, which is why the ethical argument arrived at the same time as the technique.
crispr.note: Doudna and Charpentier's 2012 paper showed the system could be programmed to cut chosen DNA; the Nobel followed in 2020. In 2018 He Jiankui used it on human embryos that were carried to term, which was condemned almost universally and brought him a prison sentence. The first approved therapy, for sickle-cell disease, came in 2023.

image.credit: Deposition authors: Nishimasu, H., Ishitani, R., Nureki, O.; Visualization author: Synpath

deep-learning.summary: Neural networks trained on very large datasets moved from a research approach to the method behind image recognition, translation, protein structure prediction and systems that produce fluent language.
deep-learning.significance: The methods had been published for decades. What changed was enough data and enough parallel hardware to make them work, which is a reminder of how often an idea waits for its machinery.
deep-learning.note: The bracket opens at AlexNet in 2012, the image model whose margin of victory made neural networks the default approach. AlphaGo followed in 2016, the transformer in 2017, and general-purpose language models from 2020. How far this goes is exactly the kind of question this timeline is usually written long after; it is open here because it is unresolved, not because the answer is known.

gravitational-waves.summary: LIGO measured a ripple in spacetime passing through the Earth, confirming the last untested prediction of general relativity and opening a way of observing the universe that does not use light.
gravitational-waves.significance: Einstein predicted them in 1916 and doubted they could ever be measured. The measurement is a change in length a thousandth the width of a proton.
gravitational-waves.note: Detected on 14 September 2015 and announced in February 2016 once the result had been checked; the Nobel followed in 2017. The source was two black holes of about thirty solar masses merging more than a billion years ago.

image.credit: B. P. Abbott et al. (LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration) — full list at the end of the article

paris-agreement.summary: A treaty adopted by nearly every country, committing them to hold warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to try for 1.5°C, through pledges each government writes for itself.
paris-agreement.note: Nearly universal and largely unenforceable: each country sets its own target and there is no penalty for missing it. Emissions have continued to rise since, and the 1.5°C limit is now widely expected to be passed.

brexit.summary: A referendum in June 2016 voted by 52 to 48 to leave the European Union; four years of negotiation and two changes of prime minister later, the United Kingdom left — the first country to reverse the direction European integration had run in since 1957.

upi.summary: Public payment infrastructure that let any Indian bank account send money instantly to any other from a phone, and pushed digital payment down to the vegetable stall.
upi.significance: A state-built payment rail rather than a company's product, free at the point of use, which is why it took a share of everyday payments that card networks never reached.
upi.note: Kept open as working infrastructure. By the mid-2020s it was handling well over ten billion transactions a month and a large share of the world's real-time payments by volume.

transformer.summary: A Google paper posted to arXiv in June 2017 that replaced recurrent networks with self-attention alone, and in doing so supplied the design that every large language model since has been a variation on.
transformer.significance: Eight authors, fifteen pages, and the architecture under essentially every language model since. It removed the part of the design that forced sequence processing to happen in order, which is what made training at scale possible.
transformer.note: Attention mechanisms were not new - Bahdanau and colleagues had added them to recurrent translation models in 2014. The contribution here was dropping recurrence entirely, which made the computation parallel and therefore cheap to scale on the hardware that existed. BERT followed in 2018 and the GPT line from the same year.

covid-19.summary: The first pandemic of a novel coronavirus, met within a year by vaccines built on mRNA technology that had been in development for decades.
covid-19.note: Reported deaths approach 7 million; excess-mortality estimates are roughly three times that.

mrna-vaccines.summary: Vaccines that deliver instructions rather than a pathogen, letting the body make the target protein itself — authorised within a year of COVID-19's genome being published, and now being turned on other diseases.
mrna-vaccines.significance: Eleven months from the publication of a viral genome to an authorised vaccine, against a previous record measured in years. The groundwork took thirty years and was for most of that time unfundable.
mrna-vaccines.note: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman's 2005 work on modifying mRNA so the immune system would tolerate it is the step that made this possible; both spent years with grants refused and Karikó was demoted over it. The Nobel came in 2023.

james-webb.summary: An infrared observatory a million and a half kilometres from Earth, with a segmented mirror six and a half metres across, built to see the first galaxies and the atmospheres of planets around other stars.
james-webb.note: Launched on 25 December 2021 after roughly twenty-five years of development and repeated overruns, and returned its first images in July 2022. Its deployment involved several hundred single-point failures at a distance where no repair was possible; none of them failed.

ukraine-invasion.summary: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the largest war in Europe since 1945 — which failed to take Kyiv in its opening weeks and settled into an artillery and drone war along a front of a thousand kilometres.
ukraine-invasion.note: Open because it is still being fought. The bracket opens at the full-scale invasion of February 2022; the war began in 2014 with the annexation of Crimea and fighting in the Donbas, and where to date its start is itself part of the argument. Casualty figures from all sides are unverifiable while it continues.
